{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-vt-class-std","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"4da754117498a45acdc0edabd256d96081c12271501c846ff71fc3b0421e479f","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-vt-class-std:lineage:41","source_registry_sha256":"0441bafe0dc257fd56d6bd0cd9054ad2b95889f94f5d3e5e6f98fb890bf902c4","source_liveness_sha256":"13f90fd88bb623234ea3628f2ee40ced3511148c14c82097743066ee414dd040"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Interstate driving and passing","heading":"C — Interstate driving and passing","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Interstate driving and passing (part one)

FACT_ID: sec10-F01 | anchor: A01
To avoid being blinded by oncoming headlights look ahead toward the right edge of the highway until the bright lights pass and your vision returns, a habit that also helps you spot bicyclists or pedestrians near the road edge [A01].
Why it matters: Looking right has a second benefit.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec10-F02 | anchor: A01
Interstates are multiple lane divided roads built for high speed travel, known elsewhere as expressways, throughways, turnpikes, toll roads, limited access highways or freeways, some free and some tolled [A01].
Why it matters: Six synonyms for the same road type.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec10-F03 | anchor: A01
Interstates are multi lane, controlled access roads on which you can drive very long distances without interruption, designed for quicker and safer travel, so learning to use them properly matters [A01].
Why it matters: Controlled access is the defining feature.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec10-F04 | anchor: A01
Speed change lanes run alongside the interstate for a short distance to connect entrance or exit ramps with the travel lanes and let vehicles speed up or slow down when entering or leaving [A01].
Why it matters: Acceleration and deceleration lanes defined.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec10-F05 | anchor: A01
An entrance ramp is a short one way road onto the interstate that leads to the acceleration lane, where you stay right, signal left, speed up to interstate speed, check the blind spot over the left shoulder and change lanes when the travel lane is safe [A01].
Why it matters: The five step entry sequence.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec10-F06 | anchor: A01
A driver entering the interstate must yield to drivers already on it [A01].
Why it matters: Entering traffic yields.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec10-F07 | anchor: A01
An exit ramp is a short one way road connecting the interstate to another road, and to leave you signal for a lane change, move into the deceleration lane nearest the exit and slow to the posted exit speed [A01].
Why it matters: Slow down in the deceleration lane, not on the interstate.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec10-F08 | anchor: A01
On the interstate keep your eyes moving to know what is happening around you, check the mirrors often, and avoid tailgating by using the four second rule with extra space on wet or slippery roads [A01].
Why it matters: Four seconds applies at interstate speed.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec10-F09 | anchor: A01
Let other drivers know what you will do before you do it, never slow down or change lanes suddenly, treat frequent lane changes as unsafe, and before changing lanes or passing check the mirrors, signal and check the blind spot on the side you will move to [A01].
Why it matters: Mirrors, signal, blind spot, in that order.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec10-F10 | anchor: A02
Never stop in an interstate traffic lane; stopping on an interstate is illegal except in an emergency, and then you move into the breakdown lane as far right as possible, raise the hood, tie a white cloth on the vehicle and stay inside if you need help [A02].
Why it matters: Hood up and white cloth signal for help.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec10-F11 | anchor: A02
Drive in the right lane of the interstate unless you are passing another vehicle or a sign directs otherwise [A02].
Why it matters: Keep right except to pass.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec10-F12 | anchor: A02
Do not drive when tired, since fatigue is a major cause of interstate crashes, and if you become tired stop and rest in a safe area as soon as possible [A02].
Why it matters: Fatigue is singled out for interstates.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec10-F13 | anchor: A02
Icy and snow covered interstates and their ramps are very dangerous, so slow down and drive with care, remembering that bridges and overpasses may be more slippery than the main road [A02].
Why it matters: Ramps and overpasses are the icy spots.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec10-F14 | anchor: A02
If you miss your exit never stop and back up and never use the emergency turnaround, which is reserved for emergency and maintenance vehicles; go on to the next exit [A02].
Why it matters: Crossovers are off limits to the public.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec10-F15 | anchor: A02
Never use cruise control in conditions such as rain, fog, snow or ice [A02].
Why it matters: Cruise control off in bad weather.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec10-F16 | anchor: A02
When a police, emergency or repair vehicle sits at the roadside with a flashing light, you must slow down, continue with caution and move a lane away from it as soon as that is safe, and if no lane change is possible you must pass at twenty miles per hour under the speed limit [A02].
Why it matters: Twenty under the limit when a lane change is impossible.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec10-F17 | anchor: A02
If the edge line to your right on a divided highway is painted yellow you are going the wrong way, because on a divided highway or interstate the line on your right should be white [A02].
Why it matters: Yellow on the right means wrong way.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec10-F18 | anchor: A02
To pass a vehicle or bicycle ahead, make sure you have enough distance, signal left, look to the rear in the mirrors and over your left shoulder to check whether you are being passed, then change lanes and pass on the left [A02].
Why it matters: Check that you are not being passed first.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec10-F19 | anchor: A02
At night it may be necessary to flick the headlights from low to high to low to warn the driver ahead that you intend to pass [A02].
Why it matters: The headlight flick as a passing warning.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec10-F20 | anchor: A02
When passing while towing a trailer be especially sure you are well past the vehicle or bicycle before pulling back into its lane [A02].
Why it matters: Trailer length changes the return point.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec10-F21 | anchor: A03
When towing a wide load or driving an unusually wide vehicle be especially careful when passing any motorist or bicyclist [A03].
Why it matters: Width adds passing risk.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F22 | anchor: A03
Overtake vehicles and bicycles on the left with at least four feet of clearance, stay out until the whole front of the vehicle or the bicyclist shows in your inside rearview mirror, then signal right, glance over your right shoulder at the blind spot and move back to the right [A03].
Why it matters: Four feet and the whole front in the mirror.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F23 | anchor: A03
When another vehicle is passing you, slow a little and keep right so the other driver can pass more safely [A03].
Why it matters: Being passed carries a duty too.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F24 | anchor: A03
A driver may pass on the right on a multilane road, and on other roads may pass on the right of a vehicle or bicycle that is turning or preparing to turn left when there is room to go by safely [A03].
Why it matters: The two lawful right side passes.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F25 | anchor: A03
Under no conditions may a vehicle be passed by driving off the pavement or off the main traveled part of the road [A03].
Why it matters: Passing on the shoulder is always illegal.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-F26 | anchor: A03
Do not pass on hills, on curves, at railroad crossings, at intersections or where a changed path ahead sign appears [A03].
Why it matters: Five no passing locations.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0053]

Misconceptions:
- If you miss your exit, use the crossover to turn around: false, crossovers are for emergency and maintenance vehicles; continue to the next exit.
- You may stop on the interstate shoulder to check a map: false, stopping is legal only for an emergency, in the breakdown lane as far right as possible.
- Slowing to twenty under the limit is always enough for a stopped emergency vehicle: false, the first duty is to change lanes away when safe; the slowdown applies only when a lane change is impossible.
- You may pass on the right whenever there is room: false, only on a multilane road or beside a vehicle turning left, and never off the pavement.
- When being passed, hold your speed so the pass ends sooner: false, slow a little and keep right.

Mnemonics:
- Right, signal, speed, shoulder, change: the five entry steps from the acceleration lane.
- Hood up, white cloth, stay inside: the interstate emergency stop signal.
- Yellow on the right, you are wrong: the divided highway wrong way check.
- Hills, curves, rails, crossings, changed path: the five places never to pass.

Glossary:
- Acceleration lane: the lane beside the interstate where an entering vehicle speeds up to traffic speed before merging
- Deceleration lane: the lane nearest an exit where a leaving vehicle slows to the posted exit speed
- Breakdown lane: the right side lane reserved for emergency stops on an interstate
- Emergency turnaround: a median crossover on the interstate reserved for emergency and maintenance vehicles
- Controlled access road: a highway that can be entered and left only at ramps, allowing uninterrupted travel
